## Overview

A common challenge in translating evidence from randomized controlled trials
(RCTs) to real-world practice is that trial participants may not reflect the
broader target population. Following Parikh et al. (2025), a subgroup is
"underrepresented" or "insufficiently represented" when the trial contains too
little information about it to estimate its treatment effect precisely. This
happens mainly when the subgroup is both poorly represented in the trial and
has a treatment effect that differs from the rest of the population. If such
subgroups are present, estimates of the **Target Average Treatment Effect
(TATE)** can be imprecise when the trial results are transported to the target
population. The **Sample Target Average Treatment Effect (STATE)**, the average
treatment effect over the target sample, is a finite sample equivalent version
of the TATE.

ROOT identifies these subgroups with an interpretable decision tree and
reports the **Weighted Target Average Treatment Effect (WTATE)**: the average
treatment effect in the sufficiently represented subpopulation, which can be
estimated with lower variance than the unweighted STATE.

This vignette walks through a complete generalizability analysis using the
built-in `diabetes_data` dataset.

---

## The `diabetes_data` Dataset

`diabetes_data` is a simulated dataset that mimics a randomized trial of a
glucose-lowering drug (`S = 1`) and a broader target population of adults with
type 2 diabetes (`S = 0`). The outcome `Y` is the reduction in HbA1c
(percentage points) at 6 months; treatment and outcome are observed only in
the trial.

```{r load-data}
library(ROOT)

data(diabetes_data, package = "ROOT")
str(diabetes_data)
```

The columns are:

| Column       | Description                                              |
|:-------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| `Age`        | Age in years                                             |
| `Sex_Male`   | Sex: male (binary indicator)                             |
| `Race_Black` | Race: Black (binary indicator)                           |
| `Rural`      | Lives in a rural area (binary indicator)                 |
| `BMI`        | Body mass index (kg/m^2^)                                |
| `HbA1c`      | Baseline HbA1c (%)                                       |
| `Insulin`    | Currently uses insulin (binary indicator)                |
| `CKD`        | Chronic kidney disease (binary indicator)                |
| `HeartFailure` | Heart failure (binary indicator)                       |
| `DietYes`    | Enrolled in a diet programme (binary indicator)          |
| `S`          | Sample indicator (1 = RCT, 0 = target population)        |
| `Tr`         | Treatment assignment (0 = control, 1 = treated; trial only) |
| `Y`          | Reduction in HbA1c at 6 months (trial only)              |

```{r explore-data}
# How many trial vs target population units?
table(S = diabetes_data$S)

# Treatment breakdown within the trial
table(Tr = diabetes_data$Tr[diabetes_data$S == 1])
```

### How the data were generated

Because the data are simulated, we know which covariates matter. The
simulation was designed so that the example contains every combination of
trial under-sampling and treatment-effect modification:

|                    | Modifies the treatment effect | Does not modify the effect |
|:-------------------|:------------------------------|:---------------------------|
| **Under-sampled**  | `CKD`, `HeartFailure`, `Insulin`, age 70 or older | `Race_Black`, `Rural` |
| **Well sampled**   | `HbA1c` (mildly)              | `Sex_Male`, `BMI`, `DietYes` |

The true conditional average treatment effect is
$$
\tau(X) = 1 + 0.1\,(\text{HbA1c} - 8) - 2.0\,\text{CKD} - 2.4\,\text{HeartFailure} + 1.5\,\text{Insulin} + 2.0\,\mathbf{1}\{\text{Age} \ge 70\},
$$
so the drug is counterproductive for people with chronic kidney disease or
heart failure and has a much larger benefit for insulin users and people aged
70 or older (the effects are illustrative). Trial participation is lower for
people with CKD or heart failure, insulin users, older people, Black
participants, and rural residents. Race, rural residence, BMI, and diet affect the outcome level but not the
treatment effect. See `?diabetes_data` for the full data-generating
process.

---

## Checking Covariate Overlap

Before running ROOT, it is good practice to check whether trial participants
differ from the target population on key covariates.

```{r overlap}
covariate_cols <- c("Age", "Sex_Male", "Race_Black", "Rural", "BMI",
                    "HbA1c", "Insulin", "CKD", "HeartFailure", "DietYes")

overlap <- sapply(covariate_cols, function(v) {
  tapply(diabetes_data[[v]], diabetes_data$S, mean, na.rm = TRUE)
})

knitr::kable(
  t(overlap),
  digits  = 3,
  caption = "Covariate means by sample membership (S = 1: trial, S = 0: target)"
)
```

Chronic kidney disease, heart failure, insulin use, Black race, rural
residence, and older age are all less common in the trial than in the target population. A comparison of
covariate means cannot tell us which of these differences matter for
transporting the treatment effect: that depends on which covariates also
modify the effect. ROOT answers this question directly.

---

## Fitting ROOT in Generalizability Mode

We use `characterizing_underrep()`, which is the high-level wrapper around
`ROOT()` for generalizability/transportability analyses. It expects `data` to
contain `Y`, `Tr`, and `S`, and internally:

1. Estimates transportability scores using logistic regression models (default) for
   $P(S = 1 \mid X)$ and $P(\text{Tr} = 1 \mid X, S = 1)$.
2. Constructs inverse propensity weighting (IPW) transported scores $v_i$.
3. Grows a forest of randomized trees that minimize the variance of the
   weighted estimator $\widehat{\text{WTATE}}$.
4. Selects a Rashomon set of the top-$k$ trees and aggregates their weight
   assignments by vote: by default, a unit is kept if more than two-thirds of
   the Rashomon-set trees keep it.
5. Fits a single summary tree characterizing the final $w_{\text{opt}}$
   assignments.

Because `Age`, `BMI`, and `HbA1c` are continuous, we use
`split_strategy = "random_quantile"`, which proposes split points at random
quantiles of each covariate rather than always at the midpoint of its range.
This lets the trees search over many candidate thresholds. We also grow more
trees than the default to explore the larger covariate space, and lower
`leaf_proba` from its default of 0.25 to 0.1 so that individual trees can grow
deep enough to isolate several subgroups. Because the final rule excludes four
separate subgroups, we also set `summary_max_depth = 4` so that the summary
tree is deep enough to describe it (the default is 3). By default, ROOT also
requires every candidate rule to keep at least 10% of the trial participants
(`min_kept = 0.1`). This guards against a degenerate solution: the estimated
standard error can be made almost zero by keeping only a handful of
participants whose scores happen to be similar, which a thorough search would
otherwise find.

```{r fit, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
gen_fit <- characterizing_underrep(
  data                  = diabetes_data,
  generalizability_path = TRUE,
  num_trees             = 500,
  top_k_trees           = TRUE,
  k                     = 10,
  split_strategy        = "random_quantile",
  leaf_proba            = 0.1,
  summary_max_depth     = 4,
  seed                  = 123
)
```

---

## Inspecting the Results

### Print summary

```{r print}
print(gen_fit)
```

### Detailed summary

`summary()` additionally reports the Rashomon set size, the percentage of
observations with $w_{\text{opt}} = 1$, and the unweighted and weighted
estimands with their standard errors.

```{r summary}
summary(gen_fit)
```

The **STATE** (unweighted) is the trial evidence transported to the full
target sample. The **WTATE** (weighted) restricts this estimate to the
well-represented subpopulation, where the trial provides more reliable
evidence. A smaller standard error (SE) for the WTATE relative to the STATE
reflects the variance reduction achieved by this restriction.

### Terminal node rules

The `leaf_summary` component of the returned object gives an explicit
human-readable rule for each terminal node of the summary tree, along with
the number and percentage of observations in each leaf and whether they are
classified as represented ($w = 1$) or underrepresented ($w = 0$).

```{r leaf-summary}
gen_fit$leaf_summary
```

---

## Visualizing the Characterization Tree

`plot()` renders the final characterized tree from the Rashomon set. Blue
leaves ($w = 1$) denote well-represented subgroups; orange leaves ($w = 0$)
denote underrepresented subgroups. The percentage shown in each leaf is the
share of trial units falling into that node.

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Characterized tree for diabetes generalizability analysis"}
plot(gen_fit)
```

The tree reads top-down as a decision rule. Follow the branches from the root
(all trial units) to each leaf to read the complete inclusion/exclusion rule
for that subgroup.

---

## Interpreting the Output

From the characterized tree and leaf summary, we can describe the
underrepresented subgroups in plain language:

- **Participants who use insulin** are flagged as underrepresented
  ($w = 0$), regardless of their other characteristics.
- **Participants aged 67 or older** who do not use insulin are flagged as
  underrepresented.
- **Participants with heart failure** among the remaining (younger,
  non-insulin) participants are flagged as underrepresented.
- The remaining participants, those younger than 67 who use neither insulin
  nor have heart failure, form the **well-represented subpopulation**
  ($w = 1$) for whom the WTATE is estimated.

These flags match three of the four effect modifiers in the simulation.
Insulin use, older age, and heart failure are all under-sampled in the trial
and strongly modify the treatment effect.

The age cut-off ROOT selects (67) is a few years below the true threshold of
70. Trial participation declines steadily with age, so participants aged 67 to
69 are also somewhat under-sampled, and excluding them costs little precision
because their treatment effect is the same as that of younger participants. A
cut-off a few years early is therefore a conservative choice rather than an
error.

The fourth effect modifier, **chronic kidney disease, is not flagged
consistently**. Only about 45 trial participants fall in the retained region
and have CKD, and the Rashomon-set vote excludes only some of them; they are
spread across the large retained leaf, so the depth-limited summary tree does
not split on CKD at all. ROOT is a randomized search without an optimality
guarantee, and a small subgroup like this one is the hardest to isolate:
each candidate tree must find it in addition to the three larger subgroups.
Growing more trees, or trying other seeds, makes it more likely that the
Rashomon set excludes it. The consequence for the estimand is visible in the
comparison with the truth below.

Equally important is what the tree leaves out:

- **Black participants and rural residents are kept**, even though both groups
  are clearly under-sampled in the trial. Their treatment effect is no
  different from that of other participants, so excluding them would shrink
  the target population without improving precision.
- **Baseline HbA1c**, a mild effect modifier that is well represented in the
  trial, does not appear in the tree.
- `Sex_Male`, `BMI`, and `DietYes` do not appear in the tree.

An approach that flagged subgroups by their trial participation probability
alone would treat Black and rural participants the same way as participants
with CKD or heart failure. ROOT distinguishes them because it accounts for both representation
and treatment-effect heterogeneity, which is the central idea of Parikh et al.
(2025).

### How well does the summary tree describe the ensemble rule?

The summary tree is a depth-limited approximation of the Rashomon-set vote
$w_{\text{opt}}$, so it may not reproduce every individual decision. We can
check how closely it agrees:

```{r fidelity}
trial_data <- subset(diabetes_data, S == 1)
w_opt  <- gen_fit$root$D_rash$w_opt
w_tree <- as.integer(as.character(
  predict(gen_fit$root$f, newdata = trial_data, type = "class")
))

c(share_kept_w_opt = mean(w_opt),
  share_kept_tree  = mean(w_tree),
  agreement        = mean(w_opt == w_tree))
```

The summary tree gives a readable description of the rule, but the
estimates reported by `summary()` are based on the ensemble rule
$w_{\text{opt}}$ itself.

### Checking the estimates against the truth

Because `diabetes_data` is simulated, we can compute the true STATE and the
true WTATE for the population described by the summary tree, and compare them
with the estimates.

```{r truth}
true_cate <- function(d) {
  with(d, 1 + 0.1 * (HbA1c - 8) - 2.0 * CKD - 2.4 * HeartFailure +
         1.5 * Insulin + 2.0 * (Age >= 70))
}

target_data <- subset(diabetes_data, S == 0)
tau_target  <- true_cate(target_data)
w_target    <- as.integer(as.character(
  predict(gen_fit$root$f, newdata = target_data, type = "class")
))

est <- gen_fit$root$estimate
data.frame(
  estimand = c("STATE", "WTATE"),
  true     = c(mean(tau_target), mean(tau_target[w_target == 1])),
  estimate = c(est$value_unweighted, est$value_weighted),
  SE       = c(est$se_unweighted, est$se_weighted)
)
```

The STATE estimate is close to its true value (within one standard error).

The true WTATE for the population described by the summary tree is below 1.
That population is mostly people for whom the treatment effect is about 1, but
it also retains the participants with chronic kidney disease, for whom the
effect is close to $-1$. The WTATE estimate is somewhat higher than this
true value, partly because the two are computed for slightly different
populations: the estimate is based on the ensemble rule $w_{\text{opt}}$,
which excludes some of the CKD participants, whereas the true value uses the
summary tree, which retains all of them. The reported standard errors also
treat the estimated selection and propensity models as fixed, so they can
understate the true variability. Restricting to the well-represented
subpopulation nonetheless lowers the standard error substantially, from about
0.083 for the STATE to about 0.045 for the WTATE.

The Rashomon set provides multiple near-optimal characterizations of these
subgroups. The final summary tree aggregates across all trees in the set,
giving a single interpretable rule.

---

## Key Parameters

| Parameter        | Role                                                                 | Default        |
|:-----------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------|
| `num_trees`      | Number of trees to grow in the forest                                | `10`           |
| `top_k_trees`    | If `TRUE`, select the top `k` trees by objective value               | `FALSE`        |
| `k`              | Rashomon set size when `top_k_trees = TRUE`                          | `10`           |
| `cutoff`         | Rashomon threshold when `top_k_trees = FALSE`; `"baseline"` uses the objective at $w \equiv 1$ | `"baseline"` |
| `vote_threshold` | Fraction of Rashomon-set trees that must vote $w = 1$ for a unit to be included | `2/3` |
| `split_strategy` | `"midpoint"` splits at the midpoint of a covariate's range; `"random_quantile"` splits at a random quantile within `quantile_range` | `"midpoint"` |
| `seed`           | Random seed for reproducibility                                      | `NULL` (`123` in `characterizing_underrep()`) |
| `feature_est`    | Feature importance method used to bias split selection (`"Ridge"`, `"GBM"`, or a custom function) | `"Ridge"` |
| `leaf_proba`     | Probability of stopping at a leaf; smaller values allow deeper trees | `0.25`      |
| `summary_max_depth` | Maximum depth of the summary (characteristic) tree | `3`       |
| `min_kept`       | Smallest share of trial units a candidate rule may keep (default objective only) | `0.1` |

---

## Reference

Parikh, H., Ross, R. K., Stuart, E., & Rudolph, K. E. (2025). Who Are We
Missing?: A Principled Approach to Characterizing the Underrepresented
Population. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 120(551),
1414–1423. <https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2025.2495319>
